boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Günzburg entry (9 October 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Malher's 3rd division of Ney's 6th corps against the Austrian army gathered at Günzburg under Archduke Ferdinand, with Mack directing it. The Austrian night retreat to Ulm, the capture of the Elchingen bridge by Loison's brigade in the night of 9-10 October and Haslach (B363c, 11 October) are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 20,000 men under Marshal Ney and side B (Austrian) 15,000 men under Archduke Ferdinand. By his stated rule these are the forces available for the engagement, not only those that fought, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several (scoping decision 1). He does not say which formations he counted or at what moment. His 20,000 for side A is far above every figure below for Malher's division, the only French force the other sources put at Günzburg (claims side-a-return and krauss-side-a-strength), and his 15,000 for side B far below Krauss's figure for the Austrian army there (claim krauss-side-b-strength); the passages read do not explain either difference. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'.

claims.value: Side A's return of the 6th corps at the crossing of the Rhine, in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV (late September 1805), lists its 3rd division as the 25e légère (3 battalions, 2,023 men), the 27e de ligne (2 battalions, 1,828), the 50e (2 battalions, 1,714) and the 59e (2 battalions, 1,504): 9 battalions and 7,069 men by our sum. The return's total is headed 'présents sous les armes' (present under arms). The 3rd division was Malher's: Ney's march dispositions for 17 vendémiaire give its moves to General Malher, Krauss writes 'the 3rd division (Malher)', and Alombert and Colin's columns at Günzburg are made of these four regiments.
claims.rationale: Side A's own figure for the division that fought, read from the page image. It is some two weeks older than the action and shows neither the losses of the march nor detachments: a battalion of the 27e was left at Stötzingen (claim alombert-columns), and Ney's dispositions had Malher leave posts at the bridges of Dillingen and Lauingen. The return prints no division subtotal, so 7,069 is our sum; the corps' light cavalry and artillery are listed separately and are not added. The date conversion uses the editors' own equation of 16 vendémiaire with 8 October 1805. Sending this one division to Günzburg was Ney's decision (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): '6th army corps at the crossing of the Rhine in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV'; 'total of those present under arms'; 'march dispositions for the 6th corps of 17 vendémiaire year XIV'; 'the 3rd division will at once carry the infantry troops that are at Dillingen and Gundelfingen'; 'General Malher will leave two posts'; 'of infantry to guard the bridges of Dillingen and Lauingen'; Krauss, 'the 3rd division (Malher) from Dillingen and'; 'the centre column (General Malher, General Marcognet, three battalions of the 25e léger, one battalion of the 27e de ligne, two battalions of the 50e and four guns)'; 'the left column (General Labassée, 59e de ligne)'; 'the 16 vendémiaire year XIV (8 October 1805)'.

claims.value: French statements about side B: Ney's report of the evening said the enemy was stronger at Ulm than had been believed and had received a reinforcement of 1,500 men at Günzburg. Krauss gives Ney's report in German as saying the enemy was much stronger at Ulm than had been thought and had received at Günzburg a reinforcement of 15,000 men, which came from Schaffhausen. Malher wrote that, by the prisoners' reports, the enemy took his division for the whole army, doubtless because it had itself gathered the greater part of its own there.
claims.rationale: Side A's statements about side B, kept separate. The 1,500 and the 15,000 are both read from the page images (Alombert and Colin's OCR has '4800'); the two printings of Ney's sentence otherwise match in wording (our comparison), Krauss adding that the reinforcement came from Schaffhausen, and differ tenfold in the figure. Which printing is right is not settled (open questions). Malher's statement gives no number. English renderings (ours): 'the enemy is stronger at Ulm than had been believed; he received at Günzburg a reinforcement of 1500 men'; Krauss, 'he reported: "The enemy is much stronger at Ulm than had been thought; he has received at Günzburg a reinforcement of 15,000 men, which came from Schaffhausen; it seems that Ulm will form the left wing of the enemy's line of battle." By this Ney can only have meant a line of battle on the Iller, front to the east'; 'the enemy, according to the prisoners' reports, believed us to be the whole army; he no doubt paid us this honour because he himself had gathered the greater part of his own there'.

claims.value: Berthier wrote to Ney in the night of 8-9 October that it was essential he reach Günzburg promptly. Ney's march dispositions for the 9th sent the 1st division (Dupont) toward Albeck, the 2nd (Loison) to Langenau and the Elchingen bridge, and the 3rd (Malher) to the Danube opposite Günzburg and Reisensburg and on to the bridge of Leipheim, while Gazan's division stayed at Gundelfingen despite Berthier's order; a supplementary order sent the engineer colonel Cazals to Malher with a company of workers to build a bridge and told Malher to establish half his division on the right bank. Malher's division formed three columns, under Lefol, Malher with Marcognet, and Labassée. An engineer officer's memoir says the marshal arrived at the start of the march, gave Malher some orders and left. Krauss says Ney, apparently obeying the imperial orders only reluctantly, sent one division to Albeck and a second to Langenau-Elchingen, so only one division marched on Günzburg.
claims.rationale: The chain from the Emperor through Berthier to Ney and Malher, from the orders printed by the French official history, its narrative and Krauss. Alombert and Colin judge that Ney seems more concerned with the left bank than the Emperor. The memoir is Captain Lafarelle's, printed in footnotes to Malher's report; it says 'the marshal' without naming him. Field decisions were Malher's and his brigadiers' (claim side-a-decisions). English renderings (ours): 'it is therefore essential that you arrive promptly at Günzburg'; 'march dispositions for the 6th corps of 17 vendémiaire year XIV'; 'General Loison will try to seize the bridge over the Danube at Elchingen'; 'the 3rd division will at once carry the infantry troops that are at Dillingen and Gundelfingen into the positions on the left bank of the Danube, opposite Günzburg and Reisensburg'; 'he will finally try to seize the bridge of Leipheim'; '... lay down their arms. Ney.'; 'supplementary order given to General Malher'; 'on the morning of the 9th Dupont's division is carried to Albeck; Loison's to Langenau, Malher's to Günzburg; Gazan's division, despite Berthier's order, does not cross to the right bank of the Danube and stays at Gundelfingen'; 'Marshal Ney therefore seems more preoccupied with the left bank of the Danube than the Emperor'; 'I inform you that I have just sent the engineer colonel Cazals to you with a company of workers'; 'to establish half of your division on the right bank'; 'the division formed three columns: the right one (adjutant-commandant Lefol,'; 'the centre column (General Malher, General Marcognet,'; 'the left column (General Labassée,'; 'at a short distance from our starting point we saw the enemy'; 'meanwhile the marshal arrived, gave some orders to General Malher and left'; 'extract from the campaign memoir of Antoine de Lafarelle, captain of engineers'; Krauss, 'Ney, who in these days apparently obeyed the imperial orders only reluctantly, sent not only one division to Albeck but also a second to Langenau-Elchingen, so that only one division marched to Günzburg'.

claims.value: On the field, Marcognet, reaching the woods along the Danube, met the enemy and drove him back into the island. Malher, hoping to repair the bridge, had the 25e supported by the 27e and put the 50e in reserve; when he saw that the great bridge could not be repaired he withdrew his troops to the edge of the wood. On the left, Labassée led the 59th to the bridge whose planks had been removed and across it. claims.value: Krauss's account of side B's decisions on 9 October: at daybreak Ferdinand and Mack rode to Burgau to choose a position, the plan to post the army there was dropped, and Mack chose another position from Reisensburg to Limbach. Mack then drew up a new plan to cross the Danube at Günzburg that night, and his disposition was presented to the Archduke at Günzburg at 4 p.m.; while it was being copied Ney's corps attacked. The regiment Erzherzog Karl was sent to the weakly held bridge and the Tyrolean Jäger ordered to hold up the enemy until the bridges could be secured and taken up; the dismantling seems to have been done in haste. Later Gyulai was ordered to break out across the restored Chaussee bridge and drive the enemy off. When the action had made the crossing impossible, the Archduke proposed crossing at Elchingen that night or retreating at once by Mindelheim and Landsberg or by Memmingen and Füssen; Mack rejected the second, could not decide on the first, gave up the crossing and ordered the army back to Ulm that evening.
claims.rationale: Decisions as Krauss reconstructs them from the Kriegsarchiv files. He gives several orders in the passive voice without naming who issued them. English renderings (ours): 'at daybreak Archduke Ferdinand and FML Mack rode forward to Burgau to choose the position'; 'the plan to post the army at Burgau was dropped'; 'Mack chose another position, whose left wing leaned on the Danube at Reisensburg and whose right wing lay at Limbach'; 'FML Mack had however meanwhile drawn up a new plan'; 'he at once drew up the disposition for it'; 'this disposition was presented to Archduke Ferdinand in Günzburg on the 9th at 4 p.m. While it was being copied for the troops, Ney's corps attacked Günzburg'; 'the infantry regiment Erzherzog Karl, just then entering Günzburg, was directed to the only weakly held bridge at Günzburg, and the order was sent to the division of Tyrolean Jäger still north of the Danube to hold up the enemy's advance until the preparations had been made to secure the bridges and take them up'; 'the dismantling of the bridges seems to have been carried out in haste'; 'FML Count Gyulai received the order, after the restoration of the Chaussee bridge, to break out over the Danube with 7 battalions and 14 squadrons, to drive off the enemy'; 'through the course of the action Mack's plan to cross the Danube at Günzburg had become impracticable'; 'Archduke Ferdinand therefore proposed to cross the Danube that same night at Elchingen'; 'or, since a day had already been lost for this march, to carry out the retreat at once by Mindelheim and Landsberg or by Memmingen and Füssen'; 'Mack would hear absolutely nothing of the second proposal'; 'but he could not make up his mind to the Danube crossing at Elchingen either'; 'he gave up the crossing entirely for the time being and ordered the army, in the evening, while the fight was still raging, to march back at once to Ulm'.

claims.value: Mack's plan, by Krauss, was to cross the Danube at Günzburg in the night to 10 October and march on the left bank toward Neuburg, Ingolstadt and Regensburg, to cross again and join Kienmayer and the Russians. His disposition had the army cross that night on the Günzburg Chaussee bridge, and the second Günzburg bridge and the Leipheim bridge broken at nightfall. claims.value: Side A attacked. Malher's division advanced on the Danube bridges; its centre column forded the first arm and opened fire from the island, and its left column, the 59th, crossed a bridge below the town on its beams under fire (the Chaussee bridge in Krauss), took guns and pushed as far as Günzburg before being driven back from the town. Side B's advance over the restored bridge and its cavalry charges were made against the French bridgehead.
claims.rationale: Both sides' sources describe the French attacking side B's bridges and positions; side B's counter-strokes were made inside its own position, so they do not make it the attacker. The attack carried out the Emperor's repeated order to take Günzburg and the task Ney's corps received (claim side-a-objectives), so the posture is tagged inherited; Ney and Malher chose its form (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): 'although the Emperor had repeated several times, the day before and in the night, the order to press the capture of Günzburg'; Krauss, 'the task given to Ney's corps, to seize the bridges at Günzburg, led on the 9th to the action at Günzburg'; 'in spite of the heavy artillery fire the French advanced, forded the arm of the Danube and opened fire from the island'; 'it crossed it on the beams, in spite of the enemy's artillery and musketry fire, took three guns, made 500 prisoners and pushed as far as Günzburg; but it was driven back from the town'; Krauss, 'a strong, closed French column broke out of the wood on the Chaussee, stormed over the bridge and threw the regiment Kaunitz back on Günzburg'; 'only an attack by two squadrons brought the French to a halt'.

claims.value: The passages read place side B at the Danube bridges, two of them partly dismantled, with battalions and guns at the bridge north of the town, infantry firing from the heights on the left column, and a regiment at the edge of Günzburg; side A in the woods on the left bank and on the island and, after its crossing, on the heights south of the Chaussee bridge. They name no works from which either side fought.
claims.rationale: none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed; a dismantled bridge is not a work in the brief's list. Two passages name works without showing anyone fighting from them: Lafarelle places the French position after the action 'under the walls of Günzburg', and Ney's supplementary order called for abatis and an entrenchment to cover the Reisensburg bridge after a crossing there, which no passage read says was built. open_questions: Deferred: Ney's full report of 9 October, of which Alombert and Colin quote only extracts (p. 35); GM Mayer's account and Colonel Bianchi's diary, which Krauss quotes; Krauss's map (Beilage 24). The prisoner, gun and casualty figures in Malher's report and Lafarelle's memoir (pp. 374-379) and Krauss's count of the Jäger and guns cut off at the bridge (p. 365) were seen only in the OCR and not read from the page images, so they are not recorded.

Most consequential gap: side B's own strength for 9 October. Krauss's 43 battalions, 76 squadrons, 36,000 infantry and 7,600 horse have no stated basis in the passages read; an Austrian return of 8-9 October of the kind Krauss used for Wertingen could close it, if his appendices or the Kriegsarchiv's publications print one. Side A's figure is the 3rd division's return of late September, two weeks before the action.

Which bridge the 59th crossed: Malher's report (OCR) has Labassée move on the Reisensburg bridge, Ney's supplementary order names a bridge of Reisensburg, Alombert and Colin call the one crossed a bridge below Günzburg whose existence was unknown, Lafarelle says the map showed a single bridge, and Krauss calls it the Chaussee bridge, which he says the disposition overlooked although he also sends the left column against the bridge of Reisensburg. Not resolved; no map was inspected.

Disputes kept as separate claims: Bodart's 20,000 for side A against 7,069 (return, our sum) and Krauss's 7,000-8,000; Bodart's 15,000 for side B against Krauss's army of about 43,600 (our sum of his infantry and horse); Bodart's 1 gun lost against Ney's five and Krauss's six; Ney's 800-900 prisoners against Bodart's and Krauss's 1,000; Bodart's 43 officers against the 44 of Alombert and Colin's Martinien figures (our sum); the reinforcement in Ney's report, 1,500 men in Alombert and Colin against 15,000 in Krauss, both read from the page images.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked); Alombert and Colin, t. II and t. III (the French official history, printing the returns, Berthier's and Ney's orders, Malher's report and Lafarelle's memoir, an engineer captain's account published in the Carnet de la Sabretache by the editors' note); Krauss (an Austrian history from the Kriegsarchiv files, which depends on Alombert and Colin for French orders and movements, so his French figures are not independent of theirs).
